title: Analytical Chemistry: Use of Ammonium Hydroxide and Sodium Hydroxide
tagline: Identify metal ions using characteristic reactions with NaOH and NH4OH.

overview.intro: Analytical chemistry at this level focuses on recognising certain metal cations by observing the precipitates formed with sodium hydroxide and ammonium hydroxide solutions, and noting whether those precipitates dissolve in excess reagent. Colour, solubility and amphoteric behaviour provide clues for identification. Careful observation, correct reagent addition (dropwise then in excess) and balanced equations are essential for accurate qualitative analysis.

learningOutcomes: Describe the action of NaOH and NH4OH on solutions of common metal salts.
Identify characteristic precipitate colours for selected cations.
Explain solubility of certain hydroxides in excess NaOH or NH4OH.
Write balanced equations for precipitation and dissolution reactions.
Distinguish between similar-looking ions using reagent behaviour.

learn.title: Principles of Using NaOH and NH4OH

blocks.text: Sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali that provides a high concentration of hydroxide ions, while ammonium hydroxide is a weak alkali. When added to solutions containing metal ions, they may form insoluble metal hydroxides as precipitates. The appearance of the precipitate and its behaviour when more reagent is added help identify the cation present.

Tests are usually performed by adding the reagent dropwise to observe initial precipitation, then in excess to check solubility. Some hydroxides are amphoteric and dissolve in excess strong alkali forming soluble complex salts, while others dissolve in excess ammonium hydroxide due to formation of complex ions.

items: Record colour and texture (gelatinous, curdy, etc.) of precipitates where relevant.
Add reagent slowly: first few drops, then excess.
Use clean test tubes to avoid confusing observations.
Interpret results by comparing both NaOH and NH4OH behaviour.

learn.title: Action of Sodium Hydroxide on Salt Solutions

blocks.text: With sodium hydroxide, many metal salts give characteristic hydroxide precipitates. For example, copper(II) salts give a pale blue precipitate of Cu(OH)2 insoluble in excess, iron(II) salts give a dirty green precipitate of Fe(OH)2, and iron(III) salts give a reddish-brown precipitate of Fe(OH)3. Calcium salts may give a white precipitate sparingly soluble depending on concentration.

Amphoteric hydroxides such as zinc hydroxide and aluminium hydroxide appear as white precipitates that dissolve in excess NaOH to form colourless soluble salts (zincate and aluminate). Lead(II) hydroxide also shows amphoteric behaviour. These reactions distinguish amphoteric ions from ions whose hydroxides remain insoluble.

learn.title: Action of Ammonium Hydroxide on Salt Solutions

blocks.text: Ammonium hydroxide also precipitates metal hydroxides, but solubility in excess differs from NaOH in important cases. Copper(II) hydroxide dissolves in excess NH4OH to give a deep blue solution due to formation of a complex ion, while zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess NH4OH to give a colourless solution. Iron(II) and iron(III) hydroxides remain insoluble in excess NH4OH.

Aluminium hydroxide is insoluble in excess ammonium hydroxide, which helps distinguish Al3+ from Zn2+ when NaOH results are similar. Lead(II) hydroxide is generally insoluble in excess NH4OH. Thus, using both reagents together provides a reliable identification scheme.

items.text: CuSO4 + 2NH4OH → Cu(OH)2↓ + (NH4)2SO4; in excess NH4OH a deep blue solution forms.
items.note: Complex formation explains solubility in excess ammonium hydroxide.
Amphoteric zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess strong alkali.

blocks.text: Some cations produce similar initial precipitates, so the key is to compare behaviour in excess reagent. For instance, Zn2+ and Al3+ both give white gelatinous precipitates with NaOH and NH4OH initially, but Zn(OH)2 dissolves in excess NH4OH whereas Al(OH)3 does not. This pairwise comparison is a common examination task.

Fe2+ and Fe3+ can be distinguished by precipitate colour: dirty green for Fe(OH)2 and reddish-brown for Fe(OH)3. Ca2+ gives a white precipitate with NaOH that is sparingly soluble, but typically no precipitate with NH4OH under usual conditions due to low OH− concentration from weak alkali, aiding differentiation.

items: Compare both reagents before concluding the identity of an ion.
Note whether the final solution is colourless or coloured (e.g. deep blue for Cu2+ in excess NH4OH).
Amphoteric behaviour refers to reaction with both acids and bases; in this chapter focus on excess NaOH solubility.
Write observations in sequence: with few drops, then in excess.

blocks.text: Balanced chemical equations should show formation of the hydroxide precipitate and, where applicable, its dissolution in excess reagent. State symbols are useful: (aq) for solutions, (s) for precipitates and (l) for water. Clear equations support written answers even when observations are described in words.

Practical care includes using appropriate concentrations, avoiding contamination between droppers, and observing against a suitable background. In examinations, answers should be specific: name the cation or describe the exact colour/solubility rather than giving vague statements such as ‘a precipitate forms’.

items.meaning: A hydroxide that can react with both acids and bases, e.g. dissolving in excess NaOH.
An ion formed when a central metal ion binds with surrounding molecules or ions, often changing solubility/colour.
A jelly-like solid precipitate often observed for some metal hydroxides.

questions.prompt: A pale blue precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH is characteristic of:
questions.answer: Cu2+ ions
questions.explanation: Copper(II) hydroxide is pale blue and does not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide.
questions.commonMistake: Fe2+ gives a dirty green precipitate, not pale blue.

questions.prompt: A reddish-brown precipitate with NaOH indicates the presence of:
questions.answer: Fe3+ ions
questions.explanation: Iron(III) hydroxide formed with alkali is reddish-brown in colour.
questions.commonMistake: Iron(II) hydroxide is dirty green, which is different from reddish-brown.

questions.prompt: Which white precipitate dissolves in excess NH4OH to give a colourless solution?
questions.answer: Zn(OH)2
questions.explanation: Zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess ammonium hydroxide forming a soluble complex.
questions.commonMistake: Aluminium hydroxide remains insoluble in excess NH4OH.

questions.prompt: The deep blue solution formed when Cu(OH)2 dissolves in excess NH4OH is due to:
options: formation of a copper complex ion
questions.answer: formation of a copper complex ion
questions.explanation: Excess ammonium hydroxide forms a deep blue complex with copper(II) ions.
questions.commonMistake: Sodium zincate is related to zinc in excess NaOH, not copper in NH4OH.

questions.prompt: A white gelatinous precipitate soluble in excess NaOH but insoluble in excess NH4OH indicates:
questions.answer: Al3+
questions.explanation: Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric in excess NaOH but does not dissolve in excess NH4OH.
questions.commonMistake: Zinc hydroxide dissolves in both excess NaOH and excess NH4OH.

questions.prompt: Fe2+ ions with NaOH give a precipitate that is:
questions.answer: dirty green
questions.explanation: Iron(II) hydroxide appears as a dirty green precipitate.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse Fe2+ (dirty green) with Fe3+ (reddish-brown).

questions.prompt: When testing a salt solution, NaOH should be added:
options: all at once in large excess
questions.answer: dropwise and then in excess
questions.explanation: Initial precipitation and behaviour in excess both provide important identification clues.
questions.commonMistake: Adding excess immediately may hide the initial precipitate.

questions.prompt: Which pair can be distinguished because only one hydroxide dissolves in excess NH4OH?
questions.answer: Zn2+ and Al3+
questions.explanation: Both give white precipitates, but Zn(OH)2 dissolves in excess NH4OH while Al(OH)3 does not.
questions.commonMistake: Fe2+ and Fe3+ are distinguished mainly by precipitate colour.

questions.prompt: A hydroxide that dissolves in both acids and alkalis is described as ________.
questions.answer: amphoteric
questions.explanation: Amphoteric hydroxides show dual behaviour, such as dissolving in excess sodium hydroxide.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse amphoteric with acidic or basic alone.

questions.prompt: Copper(II) hydroxide dissolves in excess ammonium hydroxide to form a ________ blue solution.
questions.answer: deep
questions.explanation: The characteristic deep blue colour is due to formation of a copper complex ion.
questions.commonMistake: State the intensity as deep blue, not just blue precipitate.

questions.prompt: The insoluble solid formed when NaOH is added to a metal salt solution is a metal ________.
questions.answer: hydroxide
questions.explanation: Hydroxide ions combine with metal ions to form insoluble metal hydroxides in many cases.
questions.commonMistake: The product is not a metal oxide in these aqueous tests.

questions.prompt: State the observation when NaOH is added dropwise and then in excess to a solution containing Zn2+ ions.
questions.answer: A white gelatinous precipitate of zinc hydroxide forms on dropwise addition of NaOH, and it dissolves in excess NaOH to give a colourless solution.
questions.explanation: Zinc hydroxide is amphoteric and reacts with excess alkali to form a soluble zincate.
questions.commonMistake: Mention both stages: dropwise and in excess.

questions.prompt: How can Fe2+ and Fe3+ ions be distinguished using sodium hydroxide?
questions.answer: Fe2+ ions give a dirty green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide, whereas Fe3+ ions give a reddish-brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide with sodium hydroxide.
questions.explanation: The precipitate colours are distinct and allow identification.
questions.commonMistake: Report the correct colour associated with each ion.

questions.prompt: Describe the action of ammonium hydroxide on copper(II) sulphate solution, first in drops and then in excess.
questions.answer: On adding ammonium hydroxide dropwise to copper(II) sulphate solution, a pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide is formed. On adding excess ammonium hydroxide, the precipitate dissolves to produce a deep blue solution due to formation of a complex ion.
questions.explanation: Both the initial precipitate and its dissolution in excess reagent are key observations.
questions.commonMistake: Do not stop at the precipitate stage; excess reagent changes the observation.

questions.prompt: Explain why Zn2+ and Al3+ give similar results with NaOH but different results with excess NH4OH.
questions.answer: Both Zn2+ and Al3+ form white gelatinous hydroxide precipitates that dissolve in excess NaOH because the hydroxides are amphoteric. However, zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess NH4OH forming a soluble complex, while aluminium hydroxide does not dissolve in excess NH4OH. This difference allows the two ions to be distinguished.
questions.explanation: The contrast in complex formation with ammonium hydroxide separates the two ions.
questions.commonMistake: Use both reagents’ observations in the explanation.

questions.prompt: Write balanced equations for the reactions of zinc sulphate solution with sodium hydroxide in drops and in excess, and state the observations.
questions.answer: With drops of NaOH: ZnSO4(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Zn(OH)2(s) + Na2SO4(aq), giving a white gelatinous precipitate. In excess NaOH: Zn(OH)2(s) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na2ZnO2(aq) + 2H2O(l), and the precipitate dissolves to form a colourless solution. These observations show amphoteric behaviour of zinc hydroxide.
questions.explanation: Equations and observations together demonstrate precipitation followed by dissolution.
questions.commonMistake: Include the second equation to explain why the precipitate disappears in excess.

questions.prompt: Compare the action of NaOH and NH4OH on aluminium sulphate solution and on zinc sulphate solution.
questions.answer: With aluminium sulphate, both NaOH and NH4OH produce a white gelatinous precipitate of Al(OH)3; it dissolves in excess NaOH to give a colourless aluminate solution but remains insoluble in excess NH4OH. With zinc sulphate, both reagents produce a white gelatinous precipitate of Zn(OH)2; it dissolves in excess NaOH to give sodium zincate and also dissolves in excess NH4OH to give a colourless complex solution. Thus excess NH4OH distinguishes Zn2+ from Al3+.
questions.explanation: A side-by-side comparison highlights the key distinguishing observation.
questions.commonMistake: State clearly which precipitate dissolves in which excess reagent.

questions.prompt: A solution gives a white gelatinous precipitate with NaOH that dissolves in excess NaOH. With NH4OH it gives a white gelatinous precipitate insoluble in excess. Identify the cation and justify with equations or reasoning.
questions.answer: The cation is Al3+. With NaOH: Al2(SO4)3 + 6NaOH → 2Al(OH)3↓ + 3Na2SO4, forming a white gelatinous precipitate. In excess NaOH, Al(OH)3 dissolves: Al(OH)3 + NaOH → NaAlO2 + 2H2O (or equivalent aluminate formation), giving a colourless solution. With NH4OH, Al(OH)3 precipitates but does not dissolve in excess because ammonium hydroxide is a weak alkali and does not form the soluble complex in the same way. This behaviour identifies aluminium ions.
questions.explanation: Matching both reagent outcomes leads to a unique identification.
questions.commonMistake: If the precipitate dissolved in excess NH4OH, zinc would be indicated instead.

questions.prompt: You are given two colourless solutions, one containing Zn2+ and the other Ca2+. Describe how NaOH can help distinguish them.
questions.answer: Add NaOH dropwise to each solution. The Zn2+ solution gives a white gelatinous precipitate of Zn(OH)2 that dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution. The Ca2+ solution may give a white precipitate of Ca(OH)2 that is sparingly soluble and does not dissolve readily in excess NaOH under normal test conditions. The clear dissolution in excess NaOH indicates Zn2+.
questions.explanation: Solubility behaviour in excess strong alkali provides the distinction.
questions.commonMistake: Note observations carefully; concentration can affect calcium hydroxide visibility.

questions.prompt: A student observes a pale blue precipitate with NaOH that turns into a deep blue solution with excess NH4OH. Identify the cation and explain the sequence of changes.
questions.answer: The cation is Cu2+. Sodium hydroxide (and initially ammonium hydroxide) produces pale blue copper(II) hydroxide precipitate. In excess ammonium hydroxide, Cu(OH)2 reacts to form a soluble deep blue complex ion, so the precipitate dissolves and the solution becomes deep blue. The sequence confirms copper(II) ions.
questions.explanation: The colour change from pale blue solid to deep blue solution is characteristic of copper(II).
questions.commonMistake: Describe both the precipitate and the final solution colour.

questions.prompt: Explain why using only one alkali reagent may lead to incorrect identification of Zn2+ and Al3+, and propose a reliable procedure.
questions.answer: With NaOH alone, both Zn2+ and Al3+ produce white gelatinous precipitates that dissolve in excess to give colourless solutions, so they appear similar. A reliable procedure is to test each solution with NaOH (drops then excess) and separately with NH4OH (drops then excess). Zn(OH)2 dissolves in excess NH4OH forming a colourless solution, whereas Al(OH)3 remains insoluble in excess NH4OH. Comparing results from both reagents prevents misidentification.
questions.explanation: Complementary reagent behaviour resolves ambiguity between similar ions.
questions.commonMistake: Always record and compare excess-reagent behaviour with both NaOH and NH4OH.

questions.prompt: A salt solution gives no precipitate with NH4OH but gives a white precipitate with NaOH that is sparingly soluble. Suggest a possible cation and state one precaution in observation.
questions.answer: A possible cation is Ca2+, which can form a white precipitate of calcium hydroxide with NaOH (depending on concentration) but often shows little or no precipitate with weak ammonium hydroxide. A precaution is to add NaOH carefully and observe against a dark background, as calcium hydroxide may be faint or sparingly soluble; conclusions should be supported by consistent observations.
questions.explanation: Weak alkalinity of NH4OH may be insufficient to precipitate calcium hydroxide clearly.
questions.commonMistake: Consider reagent strength and concentration when interpreting faint precipitates.
